context: A box on the left gives the definition: “Chaining: each bucket stores a linked list containing all the entries that collide in that bucket.” Below it is the note “Hash function: key % 100. Keys with the same last two digits collide.”

The main diagram on the right has three headings: “Index,” “Array” over a light blue column, and “Linked lists (each node is a key-value pair)” over a light green area extending to the right. The blue array column holds the head of each nonempty list. Right-pointing arrows link successive nodes whose keys collide.
description: The figure shows five nonempty buckets, 00, 37, 50, 76, and 83. Ellipses stand for the other indices and buckets, so the array has more than five slots. There are 13 key-value pairs in all. The table below lists them from head to tail in each bucket.

frames.explanation: To look up a key, use key % 100 to locate its bucket, then compare full keys along the list until you find a match or reach the end. For example, to look up 437, compute 437 % 100 = 37. In bucket 37, check 937, then 637, then find 437 at the third node and retrieve K. The links show the current list order. They do not establish the order in which the nodes were inserted.
frames.title: Collision chains in five hash buckets

result: Chaining combines a bucket array with linked lists. Any number of colliding keys with the same last two digits can coexist in the same bucket’s list without overwriting one another.
summary: Each bucket corresponds to a singly linked list of key-value pairs. Keys that give the same remainder modulo 100 land in the same bucket and are linked together in its list.
